speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called;

I wish to ask the Postmaster General in regard to the Toronto Postal Gude, which is issued every week, or every month. I quote from a letter which I received from a correspondent who is known to my hon. friend:
I enclose you a copy of the Monthly Postal Guide for this city issued by the Post Office. You will see that they have now discontinued giving the dates of the sailings of the New York ships. I had my clerks inquire at the post office today as to the New York sailings. He was told that they had no information on the subject and he could no doubt get it from the steamship agencies.
I do not intend to raise a debate on this question, but I would ask my hon. friend, will he not see to it that the Postal Guide wil] give the dates of sailings of New York steamers. I understand the department favours the Canadian route, which is natural. At the same time, any Canadian correspondent may route his letters via New York, and if the Postal Guide gave the dates of sailings it would be a material help in many cases.

I do not pretend to
speak by the book, but I am under the impression that we are not able to ascertain the New York sailings any more than we have been able to ascertain the Canadian sailings.
They are given in this Postal Guide.

We have had them
quite lately, il can state with fair assurance of accuracy, though without being too sure, that the reason tne New York sailings are not included is that we could not get them. It is only fair that the public should have the New York sailings as well as the others so that correspondents may direct their letters via New York if they

desire to do so. I will call the attention of my officers to the matter.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blomdin in the Chair.
Trade and Commerce-Salaries, rents, wages and contingencies under the Canada Grain Act, $800,000.
['I do not see why this\nshould be inserted. They are already limited to the three provinces.\nBill reported, read the third time, and passed.']

This vote is as against
$400,000 last year. On its face it is an increase of $400,000. But nearly the whole of that increase is due to the fact that we have to advance money in the operation of the Government elevator, which is turned in when the payments are made as the grain goes out of the warehouse. It is simply a matter of book-keeping, but as we had not the money in hand, we had to get an advance from the Finance Department running to about $300,000 or' $320,000. The other $80,000 is due to the larger expenses of all the different .services of the Grain Commission and its employed force.

This is not an advance
on grain purchased?

How much of last season's crop has passed through that elevator? It was in full operation during the
whole movement of the crop, I understand?

What is the capacity of
the elevator?

3,250,000 bushels. The
working capacity would be somewhere up to 3,000,000 bushels. This year, because the quality of the grain has been so different from that of the preceding year, the elevators have worked pretty well up to capacity.

As I understand it, the
purpose in view in the construction of this elevator was to exercise some measure of control on the part of the Government over the handling of grain at that particular terminal in the interest of the public, in fact in the interest of the producer.
I would like the minister to give any information he can as to the result of the operation in that direction.

I suppose the minister is bound to maintain that the operation of the Government elevator has been about as nearly perfect as the operation of an elevator could be. The Government has had not only supervision but control, and, consequently, that supervision which control gives, which is, of course, a better supervision than can be exercised by simple inspection and supervision without control. As to how it has operated, I suppose a conclusion in that regard could be reached in several ways. In the first place, with reference to the general conditions so far as those who use the elevators-the sellers and purchasers of the' grain-are concerned, in all respects the year has been a very favourable and satisfactory one. There have been less complaints than previously, and there has been a general satisfaction, I think, with the inspection and the grading, not only in Canada but in the old country as well, where these different grades have their significance. The Government operation of the elevator has been of service to the whole giain business because the Government and its officers have got that knowledge with regard to actual operation that they never could get simply by the supervision of an elevator owned and operated by

some one else. It has enabled the Grain Commission and the Government officers, by being on the inside of the operations, to get a knowledge of them that they did not possess before. That knowledge is not only good in itself, but it is valuable as a means of checking other elevators that are under the supervision of, but not owned and operated by, the Government.
Is it under contemplation to erect any government-owned elevators at any point on lake Huron or the Georgian Bay?
It is not.

On some future
occasion, I wish to place before the minister the reasons why a point equi-distant between the Canadian Pacific railway and Grand Trunk railway terminals on the Georgian bay, or rather on Nottawassaga bay, which is an arm of the Georgian bay, [DOT]would be a desirable site for the erection of an elevator.

I desire to make
some observations as to the location of an interior storage elevator in the province of Alberta. One elevator has already been located in Calgary. A very strong case has been presented in favour of the erection of another elevator in the extreme southern part of the province; I think the minister is familiar with the arguments that have been put forward on behalf of Lethbridge. I am not entering any objections to the location of the elevator at Calgary, but I would like to point out that the first city in the province of Alberta to make a claim for one of these elevators was Lethbridge, and hope has been held out that that city would be chosen for the site of the first terminal elevator in the province. Last session I was led to believe, by an answer given by the acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, that the selection rested with the Board oi Grain Commissioners. I would ask the minister to let us know whether the board decides on the location of the elevators, or whether that is a matter which is determined by the Government. The argument I want to offer is this:	The
elevator supply north of the fifty-first parallel was not used during the past season to the extent it was used south of the fifty-first parallel. The amount of grain shipped from Alberta stations of the Canadian Pacific railway from September 1 to December 31, 1913, over the Crowsnest, Cardston, Coutts, Foremost and Aldersyde
subdivisions, and the Macleod to Cayley branch of the Canadian Pacific railway, was 10,000,000 bushels. This entire volume, which was forty-five per cent of the total shipment from Alberta, had its actual movement through Lethbridge. The total amou it of grain shipped from the province was 21,300,000 bushels, and the proportion shipped south of the fifty-first parallel was 78-8 per cent of that amount, or 16,800,000 bushels. The elevator capacity in the province of Alberta north of the fifty-first parallel is 6,785,000 bushels, while the shipments amounted to 4,500,000 bushels. The elevator capacity south of this line is 4,780,000 while the shipments for that part of the province were 16,800,000 bushels. In other words, the present elevator capacity north of the fifty-first parallel in Alberta is 2,285,000 bushels greater than the shipments in 1913, while the capacity south of the line is 12,020,000 bushels less than the shipments. I point this out to show that the part of the province of Alberta which is most in need of increased elevator accommodation is the extreme southern part, the great grain growing portion of Alberta. North of Calgary there is a large mixed farming community, but in the south, up to the present time, grain growing has been the occupation of the farmer, and will be for a great many years to come, owing to the conditions which exist. That part of the country is developing; new railroads are being built, and I simply want to place before the minister the needs of that particular section of the country. The city of Lethbridge has placed its case before the minister and before the Board of Grain Commissioners, and the minister, in an answer given this year, acknowledged that Lethbridge was one of the places which applied for an interior stoiage elevator. There is a very strong feeling there, brought about by intimations during the early period of the history of the Government policy in connection with the establishment of these elevators, that this elevator should be located in Lethbridge. That feeling was induced by announcements made by some friends of this Government, and I hope the minister will see that when a second elevator is established in Alberta the claims of the extreme southern part of the province will be considered. Is it the intention of the Government to establish another of these interior storage elevators in the province of Alberta? I would be very much pleased if he would state that such an elevator is to be erected in the city of Lethbridge.

I would be very much pleased if I were able to satisfy my hon. friend by making either of the statements he asks. He has stated the position, so far as the town of Lethbridge and the district of which it is a central point is concerned, very fully before the House. All these matters have been very fully placed before myself and the department, and, I think, before the Grain Commissioners who visited that section of the country. It is difficult to say that it is not the intention to place an elevator in Lethbridge or in any other place in the Northwest. But I will be perfectly frank with my hon. friend and say that for the present year it is not intended to construct any other storage elevators than those which he has knowledge of, at Saskatoon, at Moosejaw, and at Calgary, and transfer elevators on the Pacific coast and on the Hudson bay coast for ocean shipping. Nobody doubts the fine country of the Lethbridge district; its large grain-raising capabilities; the actual results which have been gained up to the present time, and the possibilities of a much larger future expansion. At the same time I am bound to say to my hon. friend frankly that during this year there is no intention of proceeding with the construction of other elevators than those I have mentioned.
Would the minister let me know with whom the selection of the site of these elevators rests, the Government or the Grain Commission?

The Publicity Commission of Lethbridge, which my hon. friend knows, has placed this matter very fully before my department, as did, among others from that locality, Mr. Ives and Mr. Stewart, from whom I have received a number of letters, one, only a day or two ago. So that Lethbridge has not lost anything from lack of a pretty complete and thorough representation of its capabilities and desires in respect of a storage elevator. As regards the ultimate selection of sites for elevators, that rests with the Government, as it always must. The Government takes the responsibility and has to shoulder that responsibility. But I have made it a rule that, having established what I consider a competent board of Grain Commissioners, they are the experts and advisers in all these matters, and it is my duty as a minister to carry out the recommendations and views of that commission unless there be something which involves a matter of policy that the Government does not see its way

clear to adopt. But in an advisory capacity I am guided by, and am thoroughly following, the advice of my grain commissioners. I do that not only in the selection of sites and these important matters, but I do it down to the selection and control of all the employees who are engaged in the responsible work of carrying on the operations of that board. The board is held responsible by me and to a large extent by Parliament, for this work. So I think the board should have a very free hand as to who its officers and employees should be. They demand competency, and I have no right to step in between them and the competency they desire, by any wishes of my own, and 1 do not do it.

Has the'Government elevator at Fort William been found to pay its way in its operation ? The railway companies, having established elevators, have for one reason or another, preferred to withdraw from their actual operation and to lease them to other parties. What, has the experience of the Government in the operation of this elevator led them to believe is the main reason the railway companies do not themselves wish to operate ?

Does the Government
charge the same price for storage as do the company elevators?
Absolutely the same.
Do you take account of depreciation and capital?

I have presented to the committee simply the running expenses and receipts. At the end of the year we shall
know how we stand, not only as regards operating expenses, but on the whole business, which means the investment and the carrying of the investment, as well as operating expenses. I cannot prophesy as to how we shall come out in that. I can say, however, that we have built an elevator of 3,250,000 bushels capacity, and as all the accounts have been turned in and paid off, we know that the cost of that elevator reckons out at about 42 cents per bushel of elevator capacity. If my hon. friend will make investigations about other elevators, he will find that that is a very low cost. It must also be remembered that in computing the cost in that way we have taken in the purchase price of the land, $90,000. We have also taken in dredging and a certain amount of other building. If you simply took the construction cost of the elevator, it would be somewhere about 37 cents per bushel of elevator capacity.
What were tne construction expenses?

The total cost was $1,372,-
000.
I want the cost of construction only.	*

I imagine this was gone over last year in the House, but I can give it again. The total cost, as I said, is $1,372,000. That includes $90,000 for the site and $32,000 for dredging. Then there was the building of a revetment wall for protection purposes, and some trestles and such like.
Who was the architect on the Fort William elevator?
The arcnitects were Woodman & Garey. They were the supervising engineers and were paid $11,845 for supervision.
I presume that in the agreement with the contractor, certain matters would be left for the -architect's decision. Was the architect's name mentioned in the contract.
It would not be necessary.

They are residents of
Winnipeg.
Canadians?

I have never inquired
about their nationality, but my idea is that they are Canadians.
They drew the plans of the elevator.

They did not draw the
plans, they were the supervising architects.
Who drew the plans and did the brainwork in getting things ready?

The plans, if I mistake
not, were drawn by Barnett & McQueen.
Mr. KNOWLES': Of where?
Of wherever you like, almost, because they are all over. They are in Winnipeg, Fort William, and Chicago I think. Elevator building is their business *and they do a vast amount of it.
They are Americans of course.
I really do not know.
Are not their headquarters in the States?

I do not know, but I think I am right in saying that the bulk of their business hitherto has been done in the United States. They built this elevator and are building two others for us. Since my hon. friend has raised that question perhaps I may give a little information just here, pertinent to it. We called for tenders of course upon plans that had been prepared and submitted. I am informed that Barnett & McQueen are incorporated as a company in Canada.
I am sure they are.
And of all things, not surprising to my hon. friend, I am sure, when I mention it to him, Mr. McQueen himself is a Nova Scotian. You find thesd Nova Scotians everywhere.
The minister got a little lap ahead of me by saying he was a Nova Scotian and then stopping. We will take the subject up later. A good many Nova Scotians go wrong.

This is an important departure in Government policy and I think it is desirable, before this item goes through, that we should have the fullest information in regard to it. Following up the minister's statement that the rival company elevators at Fort Wnliam have the advantage of having their own r-ceiv-	.
ing elevators in the producing country, from what sources, speaking generally, did the Government elevator draw its business? Who were the people who sent their grain to the Government elevator?

It is a very difficult piece of business to trace the parentage of grain -almost as difficult as it would be to trace the religious persuasions of the shippers. But I think we may eliminate, in the first place, as we can in all the terminal elevators, the original producer of the grain to a very large extent.
Did the original producer use the elevator to any great extent?

To a very small extent, as he uses it to a very small extent in any of the terminal elevators. Before the grain reaches Winnipeg the greater quantity of it is'out of the hands of the original producer. I do not know the proportion, but a very large proportion will have passed out of his hands when it gets into the country elevator, the quantity in his hands diminishes steadily and I imagine it comes to its minimum pretty nearly when it passes through the city of Winnipeg where large buyers are operating. It is impossible to trace the origin, but it is quite apparent that a very small proportion of the grain that comes into the Government elevator, or that goes into the other elevators, comes from the original producer. I think we had the largest proportion of our grain from the Canadian Pacific railway, the Saskatchewan Operative Company, and the Canadian Northern railway line which runs out from there.

There was an idea that
the establishment of a Government elevator at the terminal would have a tendency to encourage the direct shipment of grain in car lots, by the farmers. In other words, it was thought that it would eliminate the middleman to a certain extent, and I was anxious to know how far that result had been achieved. If there is not some result in that direction one of the objects that were aimed at will not have been attained. Does the minister think there is a possibility of the Government elevator suffering from the philanthropic operation of adjoining or adjacent elevators to such an extent as to seriously minimize its usefulness? That was the condition in the case of the railway elevators, and that was why they desired to allow the operation of these elevators to pass out of their hands. It was because grain companies owning line eleva-

tors were able practically to iboycott them, and I would like to know from the minister if the knowledge he has received so far would lead him to think that there was a possibility of such a thing occurring in the case of the Government elevator.

I think there are other
factors which tend to make it 4 p.m. very difficult, if not impossible, for farmers to ship as far as the terminal elevators. After harvesting their grain they are in many cases pressed for returns, and on that account they put their grain into a position to give them returns just as soon as possible. Some will sell to the street buyers, others who are less pressed may sell to the country elevator, others will load it on their platforms and send it through to Winnipeg and have it sold by the Grain Growers' Grain Company or by a commission man. But until farmers are a little more able than in the average they seem to be to-day to wait a considerable time for their returns, I do not think we will see very much of their grain sent by them through to the terminal elevators at the head of the lakes. In proportion as they do get into that position I believe there will be an inducement to them to hold their grain for a better price, and, having come to the conclusion to hold it at the terminal either for a longer or a shorter time, I think they will be disposed to put it into the keeping of the Government elevator in preference to the keeping of a grain company, unless the co-operative principle, or the class principle if you have a mind to call it so, induces them to join for their own purposes in buying companies, or to entrust their grain for sale to the Grain Growers' Grain Company. The Grain Growers' Grain Company have now a terminal at Fort William. There is this much, however, that I think we may say that differentiates the position to-day from the position three or four years ago. We have now four elements, where before we had only two. We have a company controlled by the producers themselves, the first cousin, so to speak, of the producers, which is in the grain business and which has a terminal of its own. That gives to all those who have faith in themselves and in the companies formed from amongst themselves a source of output and storage independent of the grain or transportation companies.
We have the Government elevators and we have the transportation companies' eleva-
16.11
tors outside of the companies' elevators of which I have not spoken. Therefore we have four elements, the experience and the operation of which have tended to make a very much better condition in the grain transport than if we only had the two elements we had formerly. My hon. friend sees what I have in mind, although I have not expressed it very clearly.
Certainly.

My hon. friend states
that a great deal of this large increase is temporary and will come back in storage charges. What will he the net cost of the grain commission, salaries, rents, wages and contingencies under the Canada Grain Act, after the returns of which my hon. friend spoke?

I will give my hon. friend a statement that will be inclusive, and he can take from it what information he desires.
In the eastern division the Salaries last year amounted to $12,780; in the western division the salaries amounted to $78,921, or a total of $91,701. The Board of Grain Commissioners cost $19,603. Adding that to the preceding, it gives for salaries $111,304 The largest cost of the western division is in the wages and contingencies which amounted to $211,941. In the eastern division, the contingencies-I gave the salaries before-amounted to $3,455. These were distributed between Montreal, Toronto, Peterborough, Kingston and Quebec. Out of that about $550 has to be taken that does not belong to the Grain Act. That would leave about $3,000 for the contingencies of the eastern division as regards grain.
The travelling expenses of the Board oi Grain Commissioners amounted to $3,855. Offices had to be got and furnished for the Grain Commission and the total for that, together with the contingencies of the office, amounted to $15,032. The printing and stationery amounted to $14,741. These are the principal items of the cost of the eastern and of the western divisions last year. For 1912-13, the cost in all amounted to $340,294. For the present fiscal year, up to January 31, the cost in all is $387,827. The fees collected in 1912-13 were $330,530. The fees collected up to January 31, of this year, are $420,077.
In 1911-12 there were 154,005 cars of grain inspected, in 1912-13 192,720 cars, and in 1913-14 up to January 31, there were 193,342 cars of grain inspected, leaving two months yet of inspection.

As to the contents, the number of bushels inspected for ten months for the current year is 244,782,000 as against last year's total of 241,405,000, as against 1907-08 of 98,000,000, showing the very great progress in the product and in the inspection.
For 1913-14 the expenditure of the Grain Commission was $387,827 and the fees collected were $420,077. Am I to understand that the fees more than paid the total cost of the Grain Commission?

We are not yet where we can say whether they will or not. In thii3 case, as in the case of the elevators, you have the fat portion of the year in the way of fees gone, but you still have expenses until the fiscal year is over. In 1912-13, the deficit was nearly $10,000.
That would be the total cost?
Yes. This year we cannot tell what it is, although we hope to come out pretty nearly even.
If the minister makes a large profit this year on this business, what is he going to do with it?

One thing that I think ought to be done, if the House will agree, is that the Finance Minister and the Grain Commission ought to have a good long holiday with a little to spend to requite them for the hard work they have put in to bring about this state of affairs. But I know the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) will not subscribe to that. If there were a substantial profit, year by year, there are several things that might be done with it. If that profit covered maintenance, depreciation and other necessary items, and a surplus over, we might turn that surplus back on capital and diminish the capital account. What actually takes places is that this money goes into the consolidated revenue fund.

The information the
minister has given us on the basis of his present knowledge would seem to bear out the view that was held, I think I may say, by the late Government in regard to terminal elevators, namely, that if it was intended that the Government should control the terminal business, it would have to control and operate all the elevators, and that it would not be dealing adequately with the situation to control less than the whole, for the reasons that have been brought up in the little discussion that the minister and I have just had

across the floor. That is to say, the position of the other elevators and the advantages they have in carrying on business might have the effect of minimizing the usefulness of the Government elevator. As a matter of fact, instead of the erection of this elevator putting the Government in control of the situation at the lake terminals, as I gather from the information given by the minister, the Government in the matter of this elevator is under control of the circumstances as they exist. We have not secured control of the situation, but the situation still controls us, notwithstanding the expenses that have 'been made. No doubt, the elevator has served a useful purpose as a means of education, but I think the information given by the minister would indicate that it has not got beyond that, and the chances are that it will never go beyond it.

Whatever may be our
theories and prepossessions, every one of these steps taken is of the nature of an experiment. That, I think, my hon. friend will accept. He and I and other men are free in a sense, but we are wonderfully under control of conditions and circumstances, even the best and strongest of us. It is safe to say that the Government never could absolutely control the whole situation until it went back alongside the farmer and took possession of all the means of storage and transit of grain from the country elevator clear up to the other side of the ocean, where the grain finds a market. But I do not admit that the experiment made with the Government elevators, and the result of the operation, though that operation has covered but a brief time, has not had an excellent effect in putting us even with the situation, and next to the inner situation of things, and also in establishing what you might call a model elevator which is at the command of the public for what benefits they can derive from it.
I have mentioned I think all that the disadvantages, or if you like to call them so, the handicaps, of the Government elevator. On the other hand, I think it is a good asset simply because it is a Government elevator and is operated by expert men and has absolutely no self-interest in its operation. I think that in that respect it is doing a good service. The whole matter of Government elevators, internal and terminal, and the operation of those elevators, is in the experimental stage. We are putting our money into it and our efforts also,

and a good deal of brains and a good deal of application, in order to see how it will work out. It may not succeed to the extent of fulfilling the anticipations of all its former friends, but I am certain that it will succeed so far as to establish itself as a beneficent force in the operation of the Grain Act.
Might not the Government elevators at Calgary and Saskatoon act as feeders to that at the head of the lakes?
If the hon. gentleman does not mind, this item deals wholly with administration. The subject to which he refers will come up on the next item.

If I remember well, when the minister (Mr. Foster) made his speech in introducing the Grain Act, two years ago, he spoke of doing justice to the. elevators at the head of the lakes, and said that in his opinion they were a pretty fair lot of people and did their business with fair honesty and competency. He says to-day, and of course it is quite true, that he has now had the opportunity of seeing the inner-workings of this trade. No doubt if there were undesirable practices there he would have a chance to see them. Is his mind as favourably disposed to these men as before, now that he has been in the field of experience ?

I stated that we had had only a few months of operation, and that it is impossible to gauge the situation fairly until we have been in operation for at least one full year. There are parts of the operation of an elevator that we have not come to yet, as the .hon. gentleman knows, and it will take us a year at the very least to learn the operations which are carried on in an elevator. But I think that, broadly speaking, elevator men average up with others. There are two things to be noticed. In the first place, if we put a Government elevator there, operated in the most modern way, there will be an influence by example. The elevator men will feel that they have to make good because they are alongside of people who are making good, and who have no other aim but to make good. Then, they will feel that they are before public ' opinion, and there is a chance to contrast them with the Government elevator, and they will be on their good behaviour,-yes, on their better behaviour, because of their sensitiveness to public opinion. More than that, the work of a good strong board of 105
grain commissioners on the spot will, I tlink, afford an example and control and will have a good influence. There are none of us so good but that a little bit of hedging or restriction, either direct or coming from the future, is necessary to make us a little better.

I do not wish to say
anything critical with regard to this matter, but so far as I can make out, the minister says that because a Government elevator is operated by three commissioners and their employees, in some way the ordinary grain companies doing business in Fort William will be prevented rrom applying to their operations the ordinary tricks of the trade. I do not see why the hon. minister is so optimistic on tnat point. He says further that because these gentlemen are living right in Fort William, the fear of the Lord-for if the minister's words meant anything, they meant that- would in some way be kept before them. I do not think that his words carry conviction with them. My understanding was that the operation of the elevator there by the Government would tend to disclose the tricks of the trade that the other people were supposed to be carrying on, by which the farmers did not have justice done to them, and that the Government elevator would not indulge in such tricks of the trade, but would be run upon an entirely different basis. As far as I understand the remarks of the minister, he is unable to tell us that there is any trick of the trade used by the other corporations that he does not adopt himself. Of course, I do not mean to say that he has adopted them, but he1 is not able to show any difference in operation; he is simply operating this elevator the same as any company would operate it, and there is no more benefit to the people than ir any body of honourable gentlemen constituted themselves into a company and started a good elevator there, paying a million and a quarter for it. Is not that a fair statement of what the thing amounts to?
I think another commentator could make a little change in the marginal references, if he tried to do so.
Marginal references are not admitted in court.

I think it is fair to say that if you have the directing body of a Government grain system at the site of these terminal elevators, where they are in close proximity to and in constant conference with their supervising officers and the



machinery generally of the elevator, it goes without saying that, if these men are alive to their work, a better and stronger influence is exerted than if the minister of the department tries to do the work through a sub-officer, the minister being a thousand miles away and the sub-officer being at the place of business. I do not know that the men who are running the Canadian Pacific elevator there, for instance, are worse than the common run of humanity. The members of the Grain Growers' Grain Company, who run the Grain Growers' terminal there, are, I fancy, a good sample of their class of humanity. I would not, I mean, approach the matter with the idea of being suspicious, but everything that close supervision and careful attention can do to keep the methods in strict conjunction with the law is being done, and I think that in itself is a good influence.
Is it the policy of the Government to develop Government control and operation of the elevator business at Fort William, or is it not?

At present it is the Government's intention to test out the matter of Government terminal elevator operation at the head of the Great Lakes, to test out the system of internal storage elevators in certain strategic points in the West, and to test out the terminal situation at Hudson (bay and on the Pacific coast. So far as I can speak for myself and for the present intentions of the Government, I think it would be well to test these points thoroughly before grasping for anything larger or more extended in that line. What I mean is that we proceed by steps. If this thing, working out over two or three years, approves itself to the Government or to the people as represented in this Parliament, then the question will arise as to whether it should be extended, to what degree it ought to be extended, and how.

I should like to be able to go to my constituents and say that the Government to-day through the minister, tell me that it is their purpose to carry into effect their policy of Government control and operation of the elevators at the head of the lakes. May I have the authority of the minister for making that statement to my constituents?

My hon. friend is very intelligent, and can draw his own conclusions. I have made my statement, and

I advise him to be very truthful with his constituents, and not to lead them to have any false hopes as to what may not hereafter be realized.

While I do not wish to introduce controversial matters into this discussion, at the same time, as everybody must agree, the question of handling the grain crop of the West at the head of the Great Lakes is one of our very serious national problems. It is a matter that has been before the country for its best consideration for a number of years, and was, as a matter of fact, an important issue during the recent elections which resulted in the accession of our friends on the other side to power, and, therefore, to responsibility. The hon. minister has made a very frank statement with regard to the erection and operation of the Government elevator at the head of the lakes, and has also made a statement with regard to the extent. to which that elevator can be expected to go in regulating the grain trade of the prairie West. I am bound to say, although I do not wish to say anything that will be necessarily controversial, that the statement presented by the minister to-day is not an implementing of the declaration of policy made by his leader to the people of Canada, upon which he appealed for their support in the elections of 1911. In the fourth paragraph of the address to the people issued by the present Prime Minister on August 14, 1911, he stated his policy to be 'the control and operation by the State of the terminal elevators.' There is not a saving clause; there is no intimation that this will be done after due consideration. It is a declaration of policy that the right hon. gentleman unquestionably desired the people of Canada to understand would be carried out as the result of his accession to power.
The position as stated frankly and in a statesmanlike spirit by my hon. friend is that it is sound policy for the Government to go carefully in such an important matter, to study, to feel its way, so to speak. Had there been no declaration of policy before the country, the position as he has stated it here would have been absolutely right; it was, measurably, the position taken by the late Government, that this was an important matter and it could not be properly dealt with offhand. Issue was taken by the party in Opposition with the Government at that time and the formal declaration of the head of that party is in my hands and I have placed it before the House. I say

beyond any question that however much we might commend the view that is being expressed by my hon. friend and however much we might appreciate the frankness with which he has dealt with the subject before the House, the declaration that my hon. friend has made, is only another instance in which the Government of this country has absolutely failed to implement the promises, on which it secured its return to power.

I want to have a little talk with my hon. friend if he will allow me. What is the particular use of this his last ebullition. Does he not see that he cut all the ground from under his feet when he made the admission this afternoon, that my statement outlines a policy which was in accordance with the views of the late Government when they were in office.

Yes, there was not very

My hon. friend finds fault with him because he did not guard himself. Well, w,e have done more than that, we have undertaken to go a little further than a terminal elevator at the head of the lakes. When this avenue is opened up it may be the realization of an old dream which has been dreamed by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House as well as by gentlemen on this side.
I hope it will not be a bad one.

I hope not. We dreamed it and we dreamed it so consecutively that we were forced to action, and the action has got to be carried out now to its fulfilment, and we are all anxious to see it a success. If it is a success you will have a Government owned railway that will carry the grain from the West up to Hudson bay; you will have a Government elevator there which will transfer the grain, and you will have terminal storage elevators at Saskatoon and at Moosejaw which, in connection with the transfer elevator, makes completed machinery for stor

ing and transferring your grain on to the boats. Every bit of that is under absolute Government control. There is one of the highways and outlets by which-for a quarter of a century back it has been prophesied-the grain of the Northwest will be carried. That is nearing fulfilment, and when it is fulfilled there will be a Government terminal and transfer elevator, and Government operation of both of them at that great proposed seaport and outlet for the grain of the Northwest. That is a gain I think my hon. friend will admit. Go over to the Pacific and you have the same thing being put into operation, you have a terminal elevator towards the western extremity of the grain belt and the transfer elevator on the Pacific coast, and both the internal storage elevator, and the transfer elevator itself will be under the control of, owned by .and operated by the Government. Is not that a gain? There you have two great outlets, guarding highways over which the grain can flow. What have you at lakes' head? You have a Government terminal elevator ready for the co-operative use of the people of this country. Any man who wants a fair deal and thinks he does not get it out of private interests and by private management can take his grain to an elevator which he can be sure is as disinterested in reference to his grain as it is possible to be. The Government hand is upon it, and with the Government hand upon it, so certificated and certified, his grain reaches the Canadian port where it is shipped on an ocean steamer.	[DOT]
I intend to introduce legislation this year by which the Grain Commission will be given such powers as are absolutely necessary in order that they may guarantee the safe carriage of the grades of grain that are certificated at Fort William through to the seaboard, and see that they are placed on the steamers which will carry them to the old country. That cannot be done now as our system is not complete. We have a transfer elevator at Port Colborne, built and operated by the Government, which will be a guarantee that all the grain that comes from Fort William certificated and graded, will be honestly handled and transferred to the vessels which will take it further down in order to ship it to the old country. That is a gain. When you come down to Halifax and St. John, our two ocean winter ports, we find in each a Government elevator, run, owned and operated by the Government, and under the supervision of Government IMr. G. E. Poster.]
officials. I think that constitutes a piece of machinery which is admirable in its mechanism, which is very widely distributed in its strength, and I think we had better test that out before going any farther.
There is a dawn of different things in the West. My great hope for the West, not only in its grain business but in all that pertains to it, is in the introduction and carrying out of an intelligent and honest system of co-operation among the producers and consumers of that country. We are working up to that. We have cooperation in grain companies, co-operation in elevator companies, and as the farmers see the benefit that comes from co-operation-and they will see it, if these co-operative concerns are well based and honestly managed-the co-operative system will grow in that great West and in all parts of the country. I think therein lies the solution, very largely, of a good deal of what we call the high cost of living. By the system of Government elevators, collateral advantages come to the farmer. The farmer has his grain in his wagon to-day, but he cannot get a dollar bill advanced On it from the bank. The grain has to be placed where it can be graded and certificated, and when that is done and the farmer gets his receipt he can take that receipt as a basis of security and finance himself at the bank or wherever he chooses. What has the Government done? It has removed, or will remove, that place where the transaction is completed, where the farmer gets his paper for financing himself; it has removed that place from the greatest distance, Fort William, and brought it to Saskatoon, and brought it to Moosejaw, and will bring it to Calgary. That place will be closer to the door of the farmer than it ever was before, and the farmer will be able to have his grain graded and get his papers, and consequently help himself financially much quicker than he has been able to hitherto. Is not that a gain? Before, the farmer had to carry his dead weight (bad seeds or whatever was an impurity) for thousands and thousands of miles, and it was not tried out until it got down to Fort William, and then by a system of drying and cleaning there was an expulsion of the waste and deleterious material, for every ounce of which the farmer had to pay transportation charges. The Government has removed that and is putting here and there, in the very centre of the grain production, these storage elevators with im-

proved methods of drying, cleaning, and sal ing, so that at the very shortest reason-[DOT] able distance from his doorstep the farmer can have everything that is deleterious taken out of his grain, and he has not to pay for the cost of its transit to far-distant ports. All these things are advantages, which, when they come into fair and honest operation, the people will find to be of great benefit to themselves and will appreciate them.
Who is not in sympathy with the western farmer? I know -something about the western farmer, from the experience of those in whom I am actually interested. I know the difficulties, the trials, the privations and the strenuous toil of the western farmer. He has got to come through his period. I can remembeT back to when my father, and the people who lived in the settlement where I lived, had to face conditions, when the process of raising a blade of corn was much more laborious than has to be undergone by the farmers in the Northwest. Then they had to attack giant trees of tne forest, and underneath these giant trees there was not a place as big as a spade handle where you could put a seed of corn, or a seed potato. You had to fell the trees and dig about the stumps, and you had to wait four, five or six years before you got your -stumps out, for you had no jacks and stumping apparatus then; you had to trust to Providence, pray hard, and wait patiently until the stumps came out themselves. And yet strong-handed men who go into the Northwest, and put their plough into a virgin furrow which they can travel for miles, talk about hardships. There are hardships, but other pioneers in Canada have had their hardships, as well as the people of this generation. I sympathize with the old generation; I had something to do with it, and I sympathize with the new and I have something immediately to do with it. There is not anybody on the other -side of the House who does not -sympathize, but there are some things that cannot be done and there are some things that can be done, and there is a method by which you can march up to improvement by experiment without making serious mistakes, which is far better than to make big jumps into unforeseen circumstances and events.

My hon. friend has

I am almost sure that he would have been more wary had he noticed the admirable way in which the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) evaded questions which were not under discussion. It is extremely tempting to go into a comparison of the difficulties which my hon. friend's fathers had, and the difficulties that I am having myself. After all

our fathers had their difficulties in the peculiar localities in which they had to work out their destiny.
One of them is standing up there.

No, il do not think the difficulties that faced my fathers 'before I was born could possibly be transferred to me. That is one of the pieces of illogic that my hon. friend sometimes indulges in. There was one difficulty the forefathers of my hon. friend had not, that we in the West have to contend, with to-day: they laboured anyway without the so-called blessing of the National Policy.
Oh, they were deprived of that!

They did not have the so-called blessing of the National Policy; they worked under freedom. I am perfectly certain that, if there had been this wonderful thing called a National Policy in the days when my hon. friend's forefathers were getting out the stumps on their farms, there would have been no Canada to-day. There is no man in this chamber more susceptible than I am to the eloquent appeal made by my hon. friend for admiration for his forefathers-it is only a kind of virtue by proxy that he is claiming-but, as I have said, had they to contend with the difficulty of the National Policy amongst those stumps, there would not have been any Canada. I promise, however, in my own mind not to be tempted into a discussion of these questions just now.
From a party point of view I think my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) has made a very good reply to my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). He has stated his case fairly; and if this be a good line of policy upon which he has embarked, then I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has much cause to delay the Estimates a minute. The minister extended his observations considerably, however, and I rose for a very particular purpose. My hon. friend connected his terminal elevators with the Hudson Bay railway, and presumably with the question of the Hudson bay traffic. That was bringing a very large question into the discussion. My hon. friend, from a party point of view, scored a fair point in regard to what the Government has already done; but when he introduced the question of the Hudson bay route, and the possible navigation of the Hudson bay, he raised the whole question of what the men of the West really want from this Government;
what the Government can give them, and what they can get independently of this Government altogether. I think I am more free than my hon. friend is from party bias. 1 have always taken him for a pretty strong party man; but I am willing to dispense with the chaff altogether and to put a question to my hon. friend on a point of policy. Does he think that this thing that he calls a dream is not likely to prove a bad dream, as I have just shown in an interjection I put to him? Does he really think that this huge scheme, that he has called a dream, and that he is helping to realize, offers a fair prospect of encouraging the development of the West? Has he looked at this as a point of policy? After all, the United Kingdom can only take a limited amount of the wheat that we ought to be raising in the West even if we got the whole market. We can never get the whole market, if you build ten Hudson bay railroads, until you are prepared to take the returned products to pay for the wheat. If we got the whole market and supplied all the wants of the old country, does my hon. friend limit his idea of the possible developments of western Canada to the absolute gobbling up of the old country market? Would it not have been a wiser thing, to think what the people of the West want to do, and would not that be a more feasible method of developing Canada? I did not introduce this matter; I submit to my hon. friend in all fairness that he introduced it. He was not as wary as he usually is and he tempted me, perhaps unfortunately to my feet.
I want to follow that line of thought a little further. Suppose the United States became a great market for wheat, as it will and must. The object of the present policy of the United States is to increase their manufacturing output. It has been so stated by Mr. Woodrow Wilson. He says: The role is cast upon us of seizing the markets of the world for our manufactures. If that goes on, the industrial population of that already enormous country must increase indefinitely, and I am inclined to agree with the interjection of my right hon. leader when he says that unquestionably the United States will become a great market for our wheat. If that is in the near future, is it not possible that my hon. friend's policy, which he has sketched with all that admirable skill of his, and which he has extended for the purpose of giving us a taste of his skill which is always gratifying to us on this side, is but a bad dream? Would it not have been better to

have taken in time the offer which still stands before him of the United States market? We cannot bring back the conditions of two and a quarter years ago.
I am going to take the case a little further. I have pointed to the limited nature of the market in the United Kingdom through this system which my hon. friend has described. I have pointed out what appears to me almost a certainty, that we shall have this greater possible market below the boundary line. Now I want to point out to my hon. friend that it is not in the power of this Government, or of any Government in this country, to refuse that market, unless we are prepared to commit ourselves to an export duty upon wheat, and I put that aside as an impossible suggestion or consideration, because the United States may at any time do in regard to wheat what they have done last year in regard to cattle: they may take their duty off without any consideration as to what Canada does. That is a possibility. What was the result of taking off the duty in regard to cattle? The United States at once absorbed the cattle produce of this country to such an extent that in the month of November not one hoof went to Great Britain, while 75,000 head went to the United States. My hon. friend must admit the possibility that, by a simple stroke of the pen, a president, present or future, of the United States may say: We will let the wheat of Canada in free. Suppose, and it is not an impossible supposition-we have the case of the cattle to gO' upon-that the effect of that action was to draw grain to the United States to the loss of the old country market, to a similar extent to that which has happened in the case of cattle, then I would like my hon. friend to make another speech telling me what would come of his dream.

There is a third division of opinion which is in principle, in favour of sample markets, but which has not fully made up its mind whether it is best to carry the idea out under present conditions, and to this last class the correspondent of my hon. friend belongs, they would like a sample market and would like all terminal elevators to be under the control and operation of the Government if a sample market were put into operation. It is a very difficult thing for a man sitting in this Parliament and a still more difficult thing for a man sitting in an office of administration in this country, really to get at the exact weight of opinion as far a3 these three different views are concerned. Some one who is opposed to sample markets will make the most of the argument that the farmers are not in favour of it. Others will use the argument in different ways. My own impression is that the farmers of the West are more in favour of a sample market to-day than they have been at any time in the previous history of our grain business. I may be wrong in that conclusion, but it is the conclusion that comes to my mind from impressions I have formed, from conversations I have had, and from sources of information which are at my disposal. The Government is in favour of establishing a sample market just as soon as the conditions are favourable for its being successfully put into operation. They have taken the power to do so, and it is for the Government to watch conditions as they exist, and if the time comes, within a shorter or longer period, when it is best to put a sample market into operation, they will be prepared to do so and to take the responsibilities which, of course, will rest upon them for making that move. Further than that, as to any definite date when action will be taken, I am not able to' answer .my hon. friend's question.

What knowledge has the minister of' the conditions governing the handling of the grain through the transfer elevators? That is, has the commission

been able to establish a more definite control of the grain after it leaves Fort William than formerly existed? I understood the minister to .say that further improvements were in contemplation, and I would like to have an idea as to what measure of supervision and control exist to-day in that regard. In view of the very low price of wheat from the crop last year on the Liverpool market, it has struck me, speaking as a layman and one who is not expert in the grain business, that there is a possibility of the grain having been degraded in its transfer from Fort William to the Liverpool market, and that possibly that degrading has had something to do with the abnormally low price which it received. Canadian grain was actually at a discount on the Liverpool market during part of last fall, and the reason assigned was the enormous quantity thrown on the market. That may have been the only reason, but I .should like to have my hon. friend's best information on the subject.

That would be the natural inference to make, not having looked into the facts of the case. The present condition of the Act does not give the Government through its grain board sufficient power to exercise the necessary supervision and control after the grain has left the head of the lakes and has started on its journey through the different transfer elevators and carriers towards, we will say, Montreal and Quebec. In order that that supervision shall be closer than it has been, certain amendments-not many-are necessary to the Act, and I propose in a short time to put before hon. gentlemen such legislation as I think is necessary to enable that control to be exercised. At the same time, I am bound to say, from the information which we have, that I am not at all certain that very much malpractice is exercised during that transit journey. I do not think we are justified in saying there is, either from complaints, very few of which we have received in our own country, from knowledge we have gained from the amount of supervision that we do exercise, which, I admit, is limited, or from results in the old country. At the same time the fact remains that we have not our hands on it as we ought to have, and as I think the House will be disposed to give us power to have in the future. Here, for instance, in the East, you have different kinds of elevators. You have transfer elevators that are run by transport companies, and which are, according to general opinion, said to

be the least liable to any suspicion, and the more satisfactory. Then yon have the elevators which are leased from railway companies and run by the people who lease them. You have, also, elevators that are run by grain companies, who not only pass their own grain through, but who pass the grain which has already received our certificate and warranty at the head of the lakes and which does not belong to them. There are three quite different systems through which this grain percolates, and we do not think there is sufficient uniformity or sufficient control to bring about uniformity in order to avoid tne possibility of discrimination during that transit. Then, we have direct Government elevators, such as there are at Fort Colborne, St. John and Halifax, and we have what we might call mediate Government elevators, operated by the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, and, next year, of Quebec. These are operated by the Harbour Board Commissioners appointed by the Government, and in that way they are, to a certain extent, Government elevators. In each one of them all self-interest is entirely eliminated, because the Harbour Commissioners have adsolutely no interest inimical to the grain shippers or to the grain producers. It is necessary to the perfection of the system that all those elevators should be operated on uniform bases and under uniform conditions, and that is what we are going to try to bring about. As to why Canadian grain is at low prices in the European and, especially, in the English markets, I may assure my hon. friend that that is not at all due to a degradation of the grain or to failure of the grain to turn out according to the certificates given. Never in any year of Canadian grain history has the wheat got into the markets at home in better accord with its grade and certificate or in better condition than it has this year.
I invite my hon. friend's attention to a report now being printed, made by the chief grain commissioner, who had the advantage of a month or six weeks sojourn in Great Britain during the winter. He visited the grain exchanges in various parts of the United Kingdom and held conferences with them. His report will be found to be instructive and reassuring. The report of the Saskatchewan Government Commission which finished its labours at an earlier period is of the same character. The general verdict on Canadian grain in the British market is that there never was Canadian grain of better quality at as low
prices comparatively as the Canadian grain bought this year. Grain men over there attribute this to the patent fact that where you try to dispose of all your goods in a limited time you are sure to bring the market down, even although your goods are of the very best quality. That is what happened, and there is no doubt that the producers of grain in the West this year lost many hundreds of thousands, if not millions of dollars, because of the necessity, from the circumstances over which, in the greater measure, they had no control, which led them to throw their grain with a rush into the market and in such large quantities-there never was so much marketed in so short a space of time-that the market inevitably sagged. So, whilst we have to admit the loss, we are quite sure, On the other hand, that it d'd not arise from any depreciation in quality or failure of the grain to equal certificates.
To provide for the construction, acquisition, leasing or expropriation of terminal elevators, $4,700,000.

Out of this vote we are
providing for expenditures on the elevators of which I have spoken in my previous explanations. I think I stated that all accounts had been paid with reference to the Fort William elevator so that nothing comes out of this vote for it. Then we are providing in this for the construction of the elevator at Saskatoon which is now well under way, the elevator at Moosejaw is also well under way, and the elevator at Hudson bay, to a limited extent because it is not expected that out of this vote we will be able to provide for more than the foundation of that elevator. We also provide from this for the internal storage elevator at Calgary and the transfer terminal in British Columbia.
That will go on this summer?
Yes.
To be ready for next fall?

I do not think so, but it will be ready for the 1915 crop. To be of much use for this year it would have to be ready for the reception of grain by October at the very latest and it would be impossible to do that. Generally speaking, the department came to the conclusion that instead of paying for engineers it was better to have a capable engineer of their own. They consequently employed Professor Howe, a capable young engineer, who is on salary and attends to all our engineering work. That is found to be much more

economical than paying outside engineers for plans and supervision. Professor Howe has not drawn the plans for Saskatoon and for Moosejaw, but he will, I think, prepare the plans for the succeeding elevators, not including Hudson bay. The Hudson bay elevator was in a difficult situation and we thought it better to call for tenders for plans for that elevator so we advertised for tenders. The lowest and best tender was that of the Canadian Stewart Company which is now preparing plans for the Hudson bay elevator. The same plans that are sufficient and good for Saskatoon and Moosejaw will be available for Calgary, so that we will not be at the expense of paying for any plans for that elevator. For -the elevator in British Columbia, the plans will be drawn by Professor Howe. Where we gain is in this respect is that we, in the first place, have a Government -man whose duty is to his Government first and foremost and who has no other business. He inspects at present two elevators. If we employed another man for inspection we would have to pay him for the inspection of each elevator and also pay the cost of resident engineers to supervise the daily construction. We have to employ resident engineers for daily -supervision, but the main supervision is done in all these cases by our own one man, on salary. Tenders were called for the Saskatoon and Moosejaw elevators either together or singly. Four tenders were received. One was by the Barnett-McQueen Company, a combined tender of $2,005,620 for Saskatoon and Moosejaw. Each elevator is to have a capacity of three and a half million bushels storage and working capacity. Another tender was by the Canadian Stewart Company, $2,377,000 for the two. Another was by the George A. Fuller Company, $2,417,718 and the other by the Stevens Engineering Company for the Saskatoon elevator at $1,199,000. The offer of the Barnett-McQueen Company was $1,047,000 for the Saskatoon elevator and their-combined tender was lower than their sum for each individual elevator so that Barnett and McQueen's tender was accepted at $2,005,620. After we commenced work on the Moosejaw foundation, we had a reminder of what might happen, by the tilting of -the Canadian Pacific railway elevator at Transeona, and we paid particular attention to testing the foundations there.
We paid particular attention to the foundation at Moosejaw. We had it thoroughly tested in every way known to engineers, and although our own engineer was of the opinion that the foundation uruld be 
sufficiently secure without piling, he was not able to absolutely guarantee that; so to avoid even the risk of a subsidence of the foundation, such as occurred in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway elevator at Transeona, I came to the conclusion to have the foundation piled. An additional cost of $100,000 will therefore be incurred in the case of the Moosejaw elevator, bringing the total cost up to $2,100,000. With that addition it is still cheaper by about $100,000 than any of the other tenders. Construction has been going on for two or three months, and we expect to make good progress now that spring is here.
What is the material?
Concrete.
What is the condition of the Calgary elevator?

A site has at last been obtained and delimited and the title got. The plans are just now receiving the finishing touches, and as soon as I receive them tenders will be called for and the work will proceed with all possible despatch.
Will it be ready for this year's crop?
No, but it will be ready for next year's crop.

Would the minister tell us what was paid by the Government for these different elevator sites? I am asking that because the city of Saskatoon paid $57,000 for the site on which the elevator at Saskatoon is erected.
We have paid nothing for the Saskatoon, Moosejaw, or Calgary sites. The Calgary site was owned by the Militia Department, and of course cost the Government nothing.

I want to point out to the minister that the city or Saskatoon paid the sum of $57,000 for the site which was turned over to the Government, and for which it was necessary to go to the legislature for authority. The minister tells me that he is using the Government's own property at Calgary.. If the minister will inquire he will find that at the city of Moosejaw there were some thousands of town lots handed over to the city of Moosejaw by the Dominion Government a number of years ago. The particulars are on 'Hansard,' but I have not them here. The position is that Moosejaw had received something from the Government some years ago

and handed property back to the Government for an elevator. In Calgary the Government used their own property. As the city of Saskatoon is the only city which has been required to pay out its own money, and as it never got land from the Government as Moosejaw did, it has been suggested to me that the Government might well hand over to the city of Saskatoon a piece of land which is part of a school section. I shall give the minister the particulars of the land so that he can take it into his consideration if he is desirous of putting the city of Saskatoon on the same footing as the other cities mentioned. The land to which I refer is part of section 11, in township 37, in range 5, west of the 3rd meridian. It would he available for park and other purposes. Had tne land been in the city, I am sure the minister would have made use of it as he did in the case of Calgary.
What is its area?

-I could not tell the minister offhand. Some years ago it was offered for sale at a sale of school lands, and was withdrawn with the idea that the Militia Department might take it over for a rifle range, but it was found to be too small for that purpose. Unless something is done, I think there will be discrimination against Saskatoon.

I note what my hon. friend says. It seems as if, by some reason or other we are precluded from allowing any city to exercise generosity towards Government buildings in this way. I knew nothing about the matter until my hon. friend brought it to my attention, but I will take it into consideration. My hon. friend of course will not expect me to make any definite promise now.
Does the minister propose to build three elevators, or four, with this $4,700,000.	[DOT]

I have estimated that
that is all we shall be able to expend this year. Just how much the foundation for the elevator at Hudson bay will cost, and just how much will be finished and be paid for during this fiscal year, are things I do not know. It may be that quite a sum will be expended there. It will depend entirely upon how the construction goes on, but I do not think it will be a large amount. Saskatoon and Moosejaw will take about $2,000,000. With regard to the Calgary elevator, we cannot tell yet, as no tenders have been asked for, but it will
probably not exceed the cost of the elevator at Saskatoon. That accounts for three millions. The other elevator in British Columbia may take a portion of the remaining million dollars daring the present fiscal year, but certainly it will not take all. There is ample in the $4,000,000 to carry on the construction contemplated.
Have you secured a site for the British Columbia elevator?
Not yet.

The minister said that
an addition had been made in regard to Saskatoon on account of piling.
No, that was in regard to Moosejaw.

I understand that the
reason of the cave-in at Winnipeg was that the rock foundation gave way.

It was thought that the
hard clay would carry the weight, but if I remember reading a description of the causes, it was that water had got to work and quicksands developed below the clay, and it went down and the earth came up.

My information is not
correct then. If they had got down to rock they would have been all right.
Oh yes. If you get down to the ro ck with the piling it ought to be substantial.
Would the minister tell me what proposition there is for the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific having access to the elevator at Moose-jaw?

I am afraid I cannot tell my hon. friend in detail, but arrangements have been, I think, satisfactorily concluded, whereby the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific get easy access to the elevator. The Canadian Northern railway, I think, is the road which is least favourably situated for access, but it was very difficult to get an ideal site which would accommodate easily all the roads. We did in the end agree to take a site which had two qualities at least-one that it was a good site from the building point of view, and the other that it made it possible for the two chief roads interested in the grain trade to get easy access. Of course, there is always a possibility of the others getting access although they may have a longer transfer than they would like to have.
The Grand Trunk Pacific has stated that they see daylight through the matter?
Yes, arrangements have been made. I have the plans over in the office, which, as I understand, have been practically agreed to.

I suppose that the
minister's deputy could show me those drawings if I went over there?
Quite so; they are there to be seen.

Could the minister tell me anything in regard to the gravel to be used in connection with the Moosejaw elevator? There has been considerable dissension about that. Some of the faithful in Moosejaw thought they were going to have the comfort and profit of supplying the gravel, and there has been quite a little eruption among them.'
Did they throw out any gravel?
No, and it did not throw them out of the Conservative party either. Perhaps the minister knows of it and if he does I would be glad if he would tell me what have been the ins and the outs of it.

I know nothing of the ins and the outs. The only thing I know is that our engineer was instructed to see that the proper gravel went into the making of the cement and it was up to the contractor to get the gravel.
Could I have access to such material as there is in the way of correspondence or directions which the minister gave?
My hon. friend can call for any papers, and I will be glad to bring them down.
But that involves great delay at this late period of the session.
If my hon. friend will tell me the information he wants I will try to give it to him; I have nothing to hide.
I do not say that the minister has anything to hide; he is not in the gravel business. But the fact remains *that there is a skeleton in the closet somewhere in regard to this gravel.
I am thankful it is not in the Government's closet.

Different people have
gravel that they believe is going to be used, and I would be curious to know why they did not get the patronage they expected. Perhaps if the minister has a talk with lMr. McGill he will be able to tell me something after dinner.
Yes. Do my hon. friends on the other side of the House wish to go further on this item, or would they pass it now?
I would like to have some information as to the policy that will govern these, elevators when finished. My hon. friend, of course, would be quite ready to give that, and it is all I care for.

If then we can agree that on our next item in the Estimates we will be able to take these questions up and discuss them further, perhaps my hon* friends would allow the item to go through, as, if possible, I would like not to come back to-night.
Yes.
That applies to gravel too?

To gravel too.

speechtext:

Mr, BURRELL: I do not see the hon. member in whose name this Bill .stands, but perhaps I can give an explanation which will be satisfactory to hon. members. As the hon. member for Edmonton knows, we take a general stand against private legislation which overrides an Act, and the deputy minister of the department, who is also deputy commissioner of patents, attends the meetings of the Private Bills Committee and listens to the discussion of these Bills. This particular patent was granted on the 13th of August, 1907. There was no extension of time for manufacture, and the patentees not having manufactured within the two years allowed, the patent became void. The fee was paid for the first term of six years, but no further fee having been paid the patent was also void on that account. Notice of application to Parliament for the revival of the patent was given on the 20th of December, 1913, and, owing to the length of time that had expired and of the patentee being in default, the department took the ground that there should be strong reason given before the revival should be allowed. It was established before the Private Bills Committee that the process covered by the patent was a very difficult and expensive one, also that since the granting of, the patent a great deal of experimental work had been done to bring the process to a commercial state, which had been accomplished only recently. It was shown that if the patent were revived, the patentee would start manufacturing and would add a valuable industry to the country. The committee were satisfied with the reasons given and reported the Bill. The reason for the failure to pay the second fee was established satisfactorily before the committee. It appears that it was not the fault of the patentee but of some person to whom the money was entrusted and who failed to make the payment at the time required. In the following cases patents have been revived though a longer time had elapsed than in the present case: 6-7 Edward VII, 1907, the Nichols Copper Company, and 6-7 Edward VII, chapter 96, the International Paper Company.
