The House in Committee on Bill No. 78, respecting the patent of Auto Wheels, Limited.-Mr. Fisher. Mr Blondin in the Chair.

This is another Bill regarding a patent, and I think we should have a full understanding of what the rights of the applicants are and what other rights there may be which might be effected by the passing of this legislation.

There are no other rights to be effected by the Bill. I have a communication here from a gentleman who is interested, and perhaps I can better satisfy the hon. member for Edmonton by giving the particulars contained in that communication:
A company known as the Auto Wheels, Limited of London, England, having raised the ' company's capital in London, is the owner of a Canadian patent covering the wheel. Under this patent, which is dated April 19, 1910, the patented article had to be manufactured in Canada within two years, otherwise the patent became invalid. The owners of the patent were unable to manufacture in Canada within the specified time, for the reason that they had been unable to settle on a satisfactory model for commercial purposes prior to the expiry of that period. Between the date of the patent-April 19, 1910-and April 19 1912, which is the two-year period within which manufacture should have been commenced

in Canada, they spent between $25,000 and $30,000 in London, England, experimenting so as to produce a satisfactory model for commercial purposes. On April 19, 1912, they had five experimental model wheels running on the road, and only in August of that year was it possible to decide that the model was satisfactory for commercial purposes. Under the circumstances, I think the company is entitled to have their patent revived for two years.
I may say that the committee decided to Tenew the patent for one year only.
If Parliament passes this Act, manufacture will be commenced in Canada, and it will, I think, be a substantial industry which will be to the benefit of the country. I would like to emphasize that this is an entirely new commercial article. There is nothing Quite like it, and it will not interfere with any established industry.
Is the company likely to start business itself?

Yes,' at least I am so informed by the gentleman who wrote this letter. I had an interview with him, and he is prepared himself to start the industry in Canada. I think there is no doubt of its being started within the year. I know the gentleman who is back of this; he is worth $400,000 or $500,000, and has ample capital assured in addition to that. The matter was fully threshed out in com-mitee, the members of which were unanimous in reporting the Bill.
Were any protests received with regard to the matter?
None whatever.
Will the Minister of Agriculture be good enough to give his views?

The same stand was
taken by the department; my deputy commissioner of patents set forth the facts stated by my hon. friend, saying, as was established to the satisfaction of the committee, that the patent ought to be revived, as a great deal of the experimental work has been done to which my hon. friend has referred. The article had quite recently been put in a state for manufacture, the patentee is ready to go on with it, and we could not raise any very strong objection to revival of the patent. The same practice has been observed with regard to a great many other Bills; indeed, I think that there is much good reason for private legislation in this case, if it is justified at all in others.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 76 to incorporate Les Soeurs de la Charite de l'hopital Saint Antoine de Le Pas.-Mr. Lavallee. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-incorporation:
Is there any explanation to be offered?

The object of the incorporation of the Sisters is to establish eleemosynary, educational, and charitable institutions, especially hospitals. This is a branch of a similar society which has its headquarters at St. Hyacinthe, P.Q.

I notice that the Bill
provides that:
The value of the real estate so held In Canada by or in trust for the corporation shall not exceed five million dollars.

In committee this amount was reduced to $2,000,000. Their holding real estate is subject to the laws of the province in which the real estate is situated. There is a provision in the Bill against mortmain. It is provided that they may not hold the Teal estate longer than seven years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Ten years.
It was changed to seven years in committee. They may not hold the real estate longer than seven years after it has been acquired if it is not used for the purposes for which they are incorporated.
Was the committee unanimous in reporting the Bill?

Yes. Three amendments were made; I have referred to two of them, and the other was to restrict their operations to the provinces of Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan. After these amendments were made, the committee was unanimous in passing the Bill.

Does 'that holding ,of
$2,000,000 worth of real estate apply to Le Pas?

It applies to the three
provinces. The head house will probably be at Le Pas, but they may establish institutions, throughout Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
Why were they limited to the three provinces?

The solicitor in charge of the Bill said that their purpose was to carry on operations only in these three



provinces, and he asked that the Bill be amended so as to limit their operations to these provinces.

This is apparently an offshoot of a parent organization having headquarters at St. Hyacinthe. Has not the organization at St. Hyacinthe all the powers that are supposed to be conferred by this Bill, and, if so, why the necessity of this legislation ?

I have not looked at the Act, if there is any, incorporating the Sisters of St. Hyacinthe, they have probably only a provincial charter, and I think their operations are limited to the province of Quebec.

For a great many years the Dominion Government have been voting large sums of money, running into the millions, to assist the farmers of the West in the better handling of their grain by means of terminal elevators and so on. I have no fault to find with that, but I do claim that some consideration is due to the farmers of Ontario and Quebec who are engaged in the dairy business, particularly those of eastern Ontario and western Quebec, who are conducting almost exclusively the cheese industry. Almost all of the export cheese is made in eastern Ontario and western Quebec.
And eastern Quebec .also.
Not to the same extent.

But the industry is
growing.

In the production of
cheese and butter, these two provinces stand pre-eminent in the Dominion. If it is a proper thing to build elevators for the better handling of grain, I cannot see any reason why it is not also a proper thing to build a mammoth cold storage warehouse in the city of Montreal for the better handling of dairy produce. I would like to see in that city a large up-to-date cold storage building into which cars could be run and freely and easily unloaded, and which would be so situated that the produce, after being transferred from the cars to the warehouse, could be readily handled and transferred again by crains to the decks of vessels.
The same as in the case of the terminal elevators.

On the same principle as grain is transferred from the elevator to the vessel. I do not see why we should not help this great dairy industry, particularly the cheese industry which has meant so much to these two provinces. I have made some inquiries along these lines aud I understand that it costs about one-sixteenth of a cent on every pound of cheese brought into Montreal before that cheese passes through the different stages there until it is finally placed on board the vessel. That one-sixteenth of a cent per pound may look very small to hon. gentlemen from the West who deal in larger figures in the handling of grain, but it comes out of the pockets of the farmers and amounts to quite a considerable sum. Not only that, but under the present system considerable damage is done to the cheese in the way it is handled, transferred and carted around. The boxes are very often damaged and broken, and the cheese reaches the old country market under conditions which do not give it a very good reputation there. This is something which should be taken up. Perhaps it would not be advisable for the Government to build cold storage warehouses throughout the country, but there are a fetv places at least where that might reasonably be done, and Montreal is the gateway of Canada.

How many warehouses
are in Montreal at present?
I do not know, but I know that there is no Government cold storage warehouse in Montreal.
It would be very easy to locate one in the new section of the harbour of Montreal. There are all the facilities there for erecting such a building.

The argument might
be advanced that, if the Government undertook to build a large cold storage warehouse in Montreal, they would be competing with private firms in the cold storage business. As far as I can ascertain, those in the cold storage business in Montreal have converted old buildings for that purpose and, those buildings not being up-to-date and being such that it is impossible to put them into an up-to-date condition, it costs two or three times as much to handle the stuff in those obsolete warehouses as it would in an up-to-date warehouse. The federal Government has a right to interfere with private enterprises when the latter prevent the general producers from getting for their produce a fair return. If private

enterprises are carried on in such a manner that the parties engaged in them have things entirely in their own hands, and if the farmers and the general public are losing money on that account, such a condition might justly call for interference on the part of the Government, and the Government might build such a warehouse as I suggest, Not only would it be a very useful building for the handling of perishable produce, like butter and cheese, but it would be extremely useful in the handling of fruit. There are many products that might be stored in this warehouse, not only our out-going products, but many incoming products, to great advantage and great gain to the general public. This is a matter which I wish the minister would take under consideration in connection with this question of cold storage.

Would not the
assistance that the Government is giving now be an inducement?

Providing the Government increased that grant, would that be an inducement?

It is the gateway, the commercial metropolis of Canada, and it seems to me that Montreal is one place where the Government might Very fairly consider the building of a mammoth cold storage warehouse with the very latest, up-to-date facili- * ties for handling dairy produce and other things as well. By so doing the Government would be putting money into the pockets of the producer and enhancing the reputation of our products when they reach other countries. It would also give the Government to a certain extent control over any monopolies which private interests

For some reason or other the San Francisco exhibition does not -seem to have appealed to the British Government as a desirable field for their exploitation. Notwithstanding that I cannot refrain from remarking that this Government, which attained power by reason of the slogan * no truck or trade with the Yankees,' has, within two years of their attainment to power, foresworn their principles to the extent of spending more money in order to enable Canada to trade with the Yankees than it has spent to enable Canada to trade with all other countries of the world. I must say that I commend them for their change of view but I cannot avoid pointing out how radical the change has been and how little good faith there was in the slogan when it was used.

My hon. friend must
not expect me tc accept all the conclusions he draws from that argument. The hon. gentlemen opposite have formed a practice that has become a habit of attributing statements to other people, and in time, coming to believe that these other people actually made

speechtext:
I must remind the
hon. gentlemen that the discussion is drifting far away from the item we are considering.

I wish to add a word
further in regard to the San Francisco Exhibition. This exhibition is being held for the purpose of enabling the people of the United States to increase their trade with the countries that exhibit at San Francisco. It is for the purpose, so far as those people can attain the purpose, of making Canada in terms an adjunct of the United States and our Government is going to spend more than half a million dollars in enabling them to do that.

I must not let that statement pass altogeher unchallenged, as it is not my conception of the matter. This is an exhibition of very unusual character and importance and will attract people from all over the world in laige numbers. It will give us an invaluable opportunity of bringing not only before the American people but the whole world the character of our natural resources, placed there in such shape that they will form an induce-

ment to people from all over the world, including people, if you like, from the United States to come to this country and assist us in its development, both to our profit as well as theirs.
Will the minister tell us how much was voted by the former Government for the Seattle exhibition?
Does the minister think it is, worth while spending this money if we are not to be allowed to sell our goods?

It is not a question of simply selling our goods. We have immense tracts in our western country, in my own province for instance, that are susceptible of development, and we want capital and enterprise from all parts of the world. We do not expect to sell any fruit to the western states, as the states west of the Rocky Mountains have about 15,000 carloads of surplus. We never expect to sell fruit in California or Oregon, but we would be glad to have all the people at the exhibition see what we can do and the possibilities of our country, and we would be glad to have them settle in our country and help us develop it.
How is it that Canada is going to exhibit and the mother country is not?

I cannot explain that to my hon. friend. I do not know why the British Government or the German Government or any other government does not participate in a certain exhibition. Great Britain does .not participate, as we understand it, in many of these exhibitions. At some of the exhibitions where they have participated, they simply had a building for social or semi-diplomatic purposes, not for commercial purposes at all. We are in a very different position from Great Britain.
Under which flag will our exhibits be?
There is only one flag.
I can give you more than you would like to hear.

While I do not agree and never did agree with the attitude of our friends on the other side objecting to a proper measure of satisfactory trade with the United States, I do think they are entering upon an expense in connection with the San Francisco exhibition that will need to be very thoroughly justified by results. They have taken the responsibility of making this expenditure very much larger than any ever voted before by the Dominion of Canada for any exhibition. While I would not protest particularly strongly against the amount, at the same time it certainly goes beyond what, in my judgment, would seem to be a wise expenditure. I do not wish to condemn it, but we will certainly expect very substantial results in increase of trade between the countries in order that this extraordinarily large expenditure shall be justified.
Progress reported.
